variants.intertext: Four fragments of Gilgameš were found in 1974 at Tell Meskene on the middle Euphrates in Syria, the ancient city of Emar. Three of them, and two additional pieces that surfaced later, can be ascribed to MB Emar₂. The text of MB Emar₂ is surprisingly close to SB Tablet VI, both in overall content and in textual detail. It seems likely that, like MB Emar₁, the tablet held four columns of text, and not six or more, for it reaches the halfway point of SB Tablet VI towards the bottom of col. ii: if so it began and ended at the same places in the text of the epic as SB Tablet VI. Lacuna. Column i is preserved on Fragments a (= M 9204n (Msk 7498n)+ M 9211z (Msk 74104z) + M 9301d (Msk 74159d)) (+) b (= unnumbered fragment₁) (adapted from @bib{RN117@326–329}).

%n sutâ | [... | t]arʾamī-ma
#note: See @bib{RN117@331–332}: “The most notable point of difference between the two versions is the preservation in MB Emar₂ of a whole section that is absent from the SB text (i 28'–31'). The section records a tradition that the nomadic Sutean was counted among the goddess Ištar’s paramours. According to my understanding of what is a very fragmentary passage, he was for his pains condemned by her to live the rough life of the desert camp, defeated in battle and driven from place to place. If a myth is alluded to here, it comprises a variant of Ištar’s affairs with the shepherd and with Dumuzi and makes for an appealing aetiology of the nomadism of these second-millennium pastoralists. According to the evidence from Mari and Alalakh, the centre of Sutean activity seems to have been Syria west of the great bend of the Euphrates, that is, the immediate hinterland of Emar, though they were also familiar as foreigners to the Babylonians of the period. The presence of the story in MB Emar₂ might be accounted a local interpolation pandering to western tastes. On the other hand, if it was part of the text imported to Emar from southern Mesopotamia — and we have no way of knowing what that source comprised — it is equally possible that it was retained there as material of local interest, while in Babylonia it fell by the wayside. However that may be, in the version of the poem represented by the fragments from Emar the story of Ištar and the Sutean effectively takes the place of her liaisons with the lion and the horse (SB VI 51–7), material that is not present in MB Emar₂.”

#note: See @bib{RN117@338}: “i 30'. The restoration is made in the light of the many passages in which Ištar, goddess of war, is said to break the weapons and bows of the defeated. Her enthusiasm for this task is manifested in curses in royal inscriptions (@bib{RN884@51, 127–31}: @akk{{d}INANNA be-le-et ta-ha-zi-im {giš}TUKUL-šu u₃ {giš}TUKUL um-ma-na-ti-šu li-iš-bi-ir}, ‘May Ištar, mistress of battle, break his weapon and the weapons of his army’ (Šamšī-Adad I); CḪ xliii 92–xliv 4: @akk{{d}inanna be-le-et ME₃ u₃ ŠEN.ŠEN ... a-šar ME₃ u₃ ŠEN.ŠEN {giš}TUKUL-šu li-iš-bi#-ir}, ‘May Ištar, mistress of battle and combat ... break his weapon on the field of battle and combat! (Ḫammurapi); @bib{RN884@255, 77–9}: @akk{{d}INANNA NIN {giš}TUKUL-šu₂ liš-be-er}, ‘May Ištar, my lady, break his weapon!’ (Tukultī-Ninurta I); @i{SAA} II 6, 453: @akk{{d}iš-tar be-let MURUB₄ u ME₃ ina M[E₃] dan-ni {giš}PAN-ku-nu liš-bir}, ‘May Ištar, mistress of combat and battle, break your bow in a mighty battle!’ (Esarhaddon, vassal treaty); @bib{RN54@103}, K 2652, 53–4: @akk{{d}iš-tar ... {giš}PAN-su liš-bir-ma}, ‘May Ištar break his bow!’ (Aššurbanipal)), and in a boundary stone (@bib{sommerfeld1984mittelbabylonische@303, iv 12–14}: @akk{{d}za-ba₄-ba₄ u₃ {d}INANNA a-šar tam-ha-ri-im liš-bi-ru {giš}TUKUL-šu}, ‘May Zababa and Ištar break his weapon on the field of battle!’). Less often royal victories are put down to the same activity (e.g., @bib{RN52@44, 74–5}: @akk{{d}iš-tar be-let} @i{qabli u tāḫāzi} @akk{... {giš}PAN-su-nu taš-bir}, ‘Ištar, mistress of combat and battle ... broke their bows’). Other warrior deities take Ištar’s place, if need be (Enlil, Nergal, Ninurta, Marduk, Zababa).”
